title: Solar Radiation Shapes Large‐Scale Variation in Leaf Nitrogen and Phosphorus Across Earth's Third Pole
content:
ABSTRACT

Aim

Large-scale variation in leaf nitrogen (N) and phosphorus (P) has been widely attributed to temperature, precipitation and soil conditions, whereas the role of solar radiation remains less well understood. We examined whether solar radiation represents an important macroclimatic predictor of leaf N and P across Earth's Third Pole and whether the observed relationships remain robust across sites, within species and across major plant growth forms.

Location

Qinghai–Tibetan Plateau, China.

Time Period

Contemporary.

Major Taxa Studied

Terrestrial vascular plants, including angiosperms, gymnosperms and ferns.

Methods

We compiled a dataset comprising 2931 species-by-site combinations representing 953 species across 526 sites, including 2931 observations of leaf N and 2790 observations of leaf P. We used a hierarchical modelling framework to quantify the associations of leaf N and P with solar radiation. Complementary analyses evaluated their robustness to spatial and compositional structure, while path analyses assessed their links with major climatic and edaphic pathways.

Results

Leaf N and P concentrations both declined significantly with increasing solar radiation. Solar radiation also showed the largest independent contribution among the environmental predictors considered. These negative relationships remained robust across site-level and within-species analyses and were consistently detected in both woody and herbaceous plants, although they were significantly stronger in woody plants. Path analyses further showed that strong negative solar radiation–leaf nutrient paths persisted after accounting for major climatic and edaphic pathways.

Main Conclusions

Solar radiation represents a previously underappreciated macroclimatic dimension shaping large-scale variation in leaf N and P across Earth's Third Pole. The persistence of these relationships at the site level, within species and across major growth forms indicates that they cannot be attributed solely to spatial or compositional structure. Our findings extend current frameworks of leaf nutrient biogeography beyond hydrothermal and edaphic gradients and highlight the importance of incorporating radiation into analyses of plant functional trait variation in high-radiation environments.
